metadata.title: ePIRLS 2016: South African Highlights Report
metadata.venue: Centre for Evaluation and Assessment, Faculty of Education, University of Pretoria

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This report describes an ePIRLS 2016 multiple case study in Gauteng with nine purposively selected English-language schools and one Grade 5 class per school (not a nationally representative survey). Because the study was restricted by severe sampling-frame limitations and did not meet international sampling requirements, the report does not document the use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. The achievement reporting is based on students who completed both paper-based PIRLS and computer-based ePIRLS tasks, and results are presented as mean scale scores on the PIRLS/ePIRLS reading literacy scales with international benchmark categories. For analysts using the underlying ILSA microdata, the standard approach would be to apply the IEA-provided student sampling weights and plausible-value procedures for cognitive achievement; however, this highlights report itself does not specify PV or weighting implementation details.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this highlights report are reported as mean ePIRLS online informational scores and mean PIRLS paper-based reading scores plus benchmark attainment percentages, rather than as PV-based achievement estimates produced through an explicit PV analysis workflow. The report also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusions, imputation, or complete-case rules) for questionnaire returns or for achievement scoring beyond noting that contextual questionnaire response rates were limited. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling, while PV handling is not applicable at the highlights-report level because the report does not document PV estimation/combining across plausible values.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: ePIRLS 2016 in South Africa was implemented as a multiple case study in Gauteng with nine schools. Schools were purposively selected to have English as the language of learning and teaching from Grade 1 onwards and to have a functioning computer room; originally a random sample of 25 schools was planned but was not feasible due to limitations in national/provincial information on school ICT capacity. The analytic sample comprises 277 Grade 5 learners from one class per grade selected in each of the nine schools, and results are based on students who participated in both PIRLS (paper-based) and ePIRLS (computer-based) assessments.

data.outcome_summary: This ePIRLS 2016 South Africa highlights report summarizes a multiple case study of online reading in Gauteng Grade 5 learners in English-language schools. A total of 277 learners in nine schools completed both paper-based PIRLS booklets and computer-based ePIRLS informational tasks, with mean online reading reported as 508 and mean paper-based reading as 503; the report states there was no statistically significant difference between online and paper-based achievement. Gender comparisons also showed no statistically significant differences in either ePIRLS or PIRLS. The report further finds a large difference by school computer-room utilisation: in schools where the computer room was used, both paper-based and online mean scores were reported as 541, compared with 454 and 448 respectively where it was not used (with a stated significant gap of roughly 93–100 points). Benchmarking indicates that 15–16% of learners did not reach the lowest benchmark in both modes, and a larger share attained advanced benchmarks online than on paper; the report also notes limited questionnaire return rates, which constrains contextual-factor analyses.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
